references.text: God sent prophets to the people to bring them back, but they would not listen. Zechariah, son of the priest Jehoiada, was even killed in the temple courtyard—an example of how prophets were persecuted and killed, as God's wisdom foretells in [ref:2 Krøn 24:19-21|2 Chronicles 24:19-21].
Nehemiah confesses that the people of Israel killed the prophets who urged them to turn back to the Lord, cf. [ref:Neh 9:26|Nehemiah 9:26].
Isaiah is called and sent by God as a prophet, reflecting the theme that God sends prophets to His people, cf. [ref:Jes 6:8|Isaiah 6:8].

God says through Jeremiah that He continually sent His servants the prophets to the people, but they would not listen—a central theme in [ref:Jer 7:25-26|Jeremiah 7:25-26] that corresponds with the words in Luke 11:49.
The Lord again and again sent His servants the prophets, but the people would not hear, cf. [ref:Jer 25:4|Jeremiah 25:4].

The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says He will send prophets, wise men, and scribes, some of whom will be killed and persecuted. The blood of all righteous ones shall come upon this generation, cf. [ref:Matt 23:34-36|Matthew 23:34-36].
Stephen accuses the Jews that their fathers persecuted and killed the prophets who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, cf. [ref:Apg 7:52|Acts 7:52].
Paul writes that the Jews killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets and persecuted the apostles—a direct echo of Jesus' words in Luke 11:49, cf. [ref:1 Tess 2:15|1 Thessalonians 2:15].

The listing in Hebrews of the witnesses of faith who were persecuted, stoned, killed with the sword, and driven from place to place confirms the pattern that God's messengers suffered and were killed, cf. [ref:Hebr 11:37-38|Hebrews 11:37-38].

In Revelation, apostles and prophets are called to rejoice over Babylon's judgment, because God has pronounced judgment in their favor—those who were persecuted and killed, cf. [ref:Åp 18:20|Revelation 18:20].
